lessons.title: Methods and Delegates
lessons.explanation:
# 02 · Methods and Delegates

The moment behaviour becomes a value you can pass around, most of the design
patterns you were going to write as classes collapse into one parameter.
LINQ is built on it. Dependency injection is built on it. So is every
`Where`, every event handler, every retry policy, and every callback you
will ever debug.

This module is about that one idea and the machinery C# gives you for it:
delegates, lambdas, closures, extension methods, and events.

## The mental model

### 1 · A delegate is a typed reference to a method

```csharp
Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;        // takes int, returns int
Action<string> log = Console.WriteLine;    // takes string, returns nothing
Predicate<int> isEven = n => n % 2 == 0;   // takes int, returns bool
```

`Func`'s **last** type argument is the return type: `Func<string, int, bool>`
takes a `string` and an `int` and returns a `bool`. `Action` never returns
anything. You almost never need the `delegate` keyword any more.

A **method group** can be used wherever a delegate is expected — no lambda
required, and it reads better:

```csharp
names.Where(string.IsNullOrEmpty)      // not: x => string.IsNullOrEmpty(x)
```

### 2 · A lambda captures variables, not values

```csharp
var by = 5;
Func<int, int> add = x => x + by;
by = 100;
add(1);        // 101 — it captured the VARIABLE
```

The compiler moves `by` into a hidden object that both the lambda and the
enclosing code share. That is the whole mechanism, and both the useful
behaviour (a counter with private state) and the classic bug (every lambda
in a `for` loop seeing the final value) follow from it.

### 3 · Extension methods are static methods in disguise

```csharp
"hello".Truncate(3);          // compiles to Extensions.Truncate("hello", 3)
```

No subclassing, no runtime cost, no access to private state, and it loses to
a real instance method of the same name. Because the call is static, an
extension declared on `string?` can be called on a null variable without
throwing at the call site.

### 4 · An event is a multicast delegate with the doors locked

```csharp
public event EventHandler<string>? Published;
Published?.Invoke(this, message);        // the only safe way to raise it
```

Outside the declaring class you may only `+=` and `-=`. Inside, you raise it.
An event with no subscribers is `null` — not an empty list — which is why the
null-conditional invoke is the idiom rather than a style choice.

## The details that bite

1. **A `for` loop shares one variable across all iterations.** Capture it in
   a lambda and every lambda sees the last value. Copy it into a local
   inside the body. (`foreach` was fixed in C# 5 and captures per
   iteration.)
2. **`-=` matches on delegate identity.** Two lambdas with identical bodies
   are different objects, so unsubscribing an inline lambda removes
   nothing. Keep the handler in a variable.
3. **`+=` does not deduplicate.** Subscribe the same handler twice and it
   fires twice. This is the "why is this running three times" bug.
4. **A publisher holds a reference to every subscriber.** A long-lived
   event keeps short-lived objects alive forever. Unsubscribe in `Dispose`.
5. **A multicast `Func` returns only the last result.** Combining
   value-returning delegates silently throws away every other answer —
   multicast is for events, not for computing values.
6. **Optional argument defaults are baked into the call site.** Change a
   default in a library and callers keep the old value until they
   recompile.
7. **LINQ is lazy.** `Where` returns a query, not a result. Handing an
   un-enumerated sequence across a boundary is how you get "the connection
   is closed" from a line that looks like a list.
8. **An unbounded memoize is a memory leak.** Caching by user input with no
   size limit is a slow crash, not an optimisation.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-arguments-that-behave.cs` | ★☆☆ | optional, named and `params` arguments |
| 02 | `02-func-and-action.cs` | ★☆☆ | behaviour as a parameter, and a function that returns one |
| 03 | `03-closures-and-capture.cs` | ★★☆ | the loop-variable trap, shared state, and a run-once wrapper |
| 04 | `04-extension-methods.cs` | ★★☆ | `Truncate`, `IsBlank`, `WhereNotNull` — the three you will actually reuse |
| 05 | `05-composing-functions.cs` | ★★☆ | `Compose`, `Pipe`, `Tap` — pipelines out of small parts |
| 06 | `06-memoize.cs` | ★★☆ | a cache in a closure, and why the KEY is the hard part |
| 07 | `07-events-and-unsubscribe.cs` | ★★☆ | raising an event safely, counting handlers, detaching them |
| 08 | `08-currying-and-partial.cs` | ★★★ | one argument at a time — dependency injection without a container |

Do 01–07 in order. 08 is the stretch: it teaches nothing new about the
runtime but changes how you see constructor injection.

```
dotnet run exercises/03-closures-and-capture.cs
dotnet run solutions/03-closures-and-capture.cs
dotnet run ../verify.cs 02
dotnet run ../progress.cs 02
```

---

**Stuck?** `cheatsheets/csharp-language.md` (delegates, lambdas, events) · **Self-check:** `quizzes/02-methods-and-delegates.md` · **Next:** `bootcamp/03-collections-and-linq`

csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/01-a.instructions:
**Concepts:** optional arguments · named arguments · params  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Three signatures, each showing a different way C# lets a caller say
less:

    Money(12.5m)                    → "EUR 12.50"
    Money(12.5m, "USD")             → "USD 12.50"
    Money(12.5m, symbol: "GBP")     → "GBP 12.50"

    Longest("a", "bbb", "cc")       → "bbb"     (params: any count)
    Longest()                       → ""

    Slug("Hello World")             → "hello-world"
    Slug("Hello World", separator: '_') → "hello_world"

hint: an optional parameter needs a compile-time constant default.
`params string[] words` lets the caller pass any number of loose
arguments — including none, which is an EMPTY array, not null.
csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/01-a.explanation:
Optional arguments are compiled into the CALL SITE, not the method.
That is a real consequence, not trivia: if a library changes a
default, callers keep the old value until they are recompiled. Inside
one solution it does not matter; across a package boundary it is a
reason to prefer an overload.
Named arguments let the caller re-order and, more importantly,
document. `Slug(text, separator: '_')` at the call site beats
`Slug(text, '_')` in every review, because a bare char tells the
reader nothing.
`params` receives an EMPTY array when the caller passes nothing, so
Longest can use LINQ without a null check — but note that an empty
sequence has no maximum, which is why the aggregate starts from ""
rather than calling MaxBy on nothing.
Formatting: "F2" and the ToString overloads are culture-aware, so a
German machine would print 12,50. CultureInfo.InvariantCulture is
what you want for anything a machine will read back.

csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/02-f.instructions:
**Concepts:** Func · Action · delegates as parameters  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A delegate is a value that happens to be a method. Func<A, B> takes
an A and returns a B; Action<A> takes an A and returns nothing.
Once behaviour is a value you can pass it, store it, and build it.

    ApplyTwice(x => x + 3, 10)      → 16
    Repeat(3, i => log.Add(i))      → calls with 0, 1, 2
    Adder(5)(10)                    → 15
    WhereNot([1,2,3,4], IsEven)     → [1, 3]

Adder RETURNS a delegate: calling Adder(5) gives you back a function
that adds five to whatever you hand it later.

hint: a method group can be used where a delegate is expected —
`WhereNot(nums, IsEven)` needs no lambda. Repeat's counter starts at
zero, like every index in .NET.
csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/02-f.explanation:
Func<in T, out TResult> and Action<in T> are just delegate types the
BCL declares for you, so you rarely need the `delegate` keyword any
more. The last type argument of a Func is always the RETURN type:
Func<int, string> takes an int and gives a string.
Adder is the first closure in this track. The returned lambda
captures `by` — the variable, not a snapshot of the value — and each
call to Adder creates a fresh capture, which is why two adders never
interfere. Module 02's exercise 03 is where that distinction starts
to bite.
WhereNot is generic and lazy: it returns an IEnumerable built by
Where, so nothing runs until somebody enumerates. The tests call
ToList to force it, which is exactly the habit you want — a lazy
sequence handed across a boundary is a bug waiting for a closed
database connection.
Method groups matter for readability: `WhereNot(items,
string.IsNullOrEmpty)` says the rule; `x => string.IsNullOrEmpty(x)`
says the rule wrapped in noise.

csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/03-c.instructions:
**Concepts:** closures · captured variables · shared state  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A lambda captures VARIABLES, not values. Everything below follows
from that one sentence, including the bug it hides.

    IndexReturners(3)   → three functions returning 0, 1 and 2
    MakeCounter()       → (Increment, Read) sharing one number
    Once(() => Work())  → a function that runs Work at most once
                          and returns the same answer after that

IndexReturners is the classic: build a list of functions inside a
loop, and each one must remember ITS OWN index — not whatever the
loop variable ended up as.

hint: a `for` loop has ONE variable that every iteration shares. A
`foreach` variable is a fresh one per iteration. If you use `for`,
copy the counter into a local inside the body before capturing it.
csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/03-c.explanation:
When a lambda uses a variable from the enclosing scope, the compiler
moves that variable into a hidden class and both the lambda and the
surrounding code point at the same field. That is the whole
mechanism, and it explains both halves of this file.
IndexReturners: a `for` loop declares ONE `i` for the entire loop, so
three lambdas capturing it all see the same field — after the loop
ends they all return 3. Copying into a per-iteration local
(`var index = i;`) gives each lambda its own field. C# fixed this for
`foreach` in C# 5 — the iteration variable is now per-iteration — but
`for` still shares, deliberately, because the loop needs to mutate it.
This is the stale-closure bug, and it is the same bug in JavaScript's
`var` loops and in React's effect dependencies.
MakeCounter: two lambdas capturing the SAME local is not a bug, it is
the feature. `count` outlives the method that declared it, and the
pair of delegates is a tiny object with private state — a closure is
an object with one method, and an object is a closure with several.
Once: capture a flag and a slot. The first call fills them; later
calls short-circuit. Note the factory reference is not cleared here —
in a long-lived cache you would null it out so the captured factory
(and everything IT captured) can be collected. That is how closures
turn into memory leaks.
Thread-safety note: none of this is thread-safe. For real lazy
initialisation the BCL already has Lazy<T>, which handles the race.

csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/04-e.instructions:
**Concepts:** extension methods · this-parameters · discoverability  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

An extension method is a static method that LOOKS like an instance
method. It is how LINQ adds Where to every sequence ever written,
including sequences that shipped before LINQ existed.

The code you edit is at the BOTTOM of this file, in a static class.
Fill in three of them:

    "hello world".Truncate(8)  → "hello w…"   (8 chars, last is …)
    "hello".Truncate(8)        → "hello"      (short enough, untouched)
    "  ".IsBlank()             → true
    new[]{ "a", null }.WhereNotNull()  → ["a"]

Truncate never returns more than `max` characters, and the ellipsis
counts as one of them.

hint: the first parameter carries `this` and is the value the caller
wrote before the dot. An extension on a NULLABLE type can be called
on null — the method just receives null, with no crash at the call.
csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/04-e.explanation:
An extension method is pure compiler sugar: `"x".Truncate(3)` is
rewritten to `Extensions.Truncate("x", 3)`. Nothing is added to
string, no subclassing happens, and there is no runtime cost. That
also explains the limits — an extension cannot see private state,
cannot be overridden, and loses to a real instance method of the same
name every time.
Because the call is static, calling one on `null` does NOT throw at
the call site: the method simply receives null. That is why
`IsBlank()` can be declared on `string?` and used on a null variable,
and it is the trick behind guard-style helpers.
Truncate: the ellipsis is one of the `max` characters, so the slice
is `max - 1` long. Getting that wrong by one is the entire bug class
this method exists to teach — and the "exact length" test is the one
that catches it.
WhereNotNull is generic with a `class` constraint so the compiler can
hand back IEnumerable<T> (non-nullable) from IEnumerable<T?>. It is
the single most useful extension in a nullable-aware codebase,
because `Where(x => x != null)` still gives you a sequence the
compiler thinks is nullable.
Use them for behaviour that genuinely belongs to a type you cannot
edit. Do not use them to bolt domain logic onto primitives — that is
how a codebase ends up with fifty methods on string and no model.

csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/05-c.instructions:
**Concepts:** function composition · multicast delegates  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Small functions are only useful if they combine. Three combinators:

    Compose(f, g)(x)        → f(g(x))        (maths order: g first)
    Pipe([f, g, h])(x)      → h(g(f(x)))     (reading order: f first)
    Tap(f, log)(x)          → f(x), and log saw x on the way through

Pipe over an empty list is the identity function: it returns what it
was given. That is not a special case to code around; it is what
falls out of a correct fold.

hint: each of these RETURNS a function. Aggregate over the steps
builds the pipeline once, at construction time, rather than looping
on every call.
csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/05-c.explanation:
Compose is the mathematical order — the one on the right runs first —
and Pipe is the reading order. Both exist because both are natural
somewhere: Compose reads like the formula, Pipe reads like the data
flow. Pick one per codebase and stay with it; mixing them is how a
transform ends up applied backwards.
Pipe is a fold over functions. Starting the Aggregate with the
identity `x => x` is what makes the empty case work for free, and
that is the general shape: the identity element of composition is
the do-nothing function, exactly as 0 is for addition. Note the
pipeline is built ONCE — Aggregate runs at construction, and the
returned delegate is a chain of closures, not a loop over an array.
Tap is the debugging combinator: same value out, side effect on the
way through. It is how you inspect a pipeline without dismantling
it, and it generalises to logging, metrics, and caching.
`seen.Add` as an Action<int> is a method group again — no lambda
needed, and it reads as the intent.
The related .NET feature worth knowing: delegates are MULTICAST. `a
+= b` on an Action makes one delegate that calls both, in order.
For a Func the combined delegate returns only the LAST result, which
quietly discards the others — a real trap, and the reason multicast
is for events rather than for computing values.

csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/06-m.instructions:
**Concepts:** closures over a dictionary · caching · cache keys  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Memoize wraps an expensive function so each distinct argument is
computed once and remembered:

    var fast = Memoize(Slow);
    fast(2); fast(2); fast(3);   → Slow ran twice, not three times

Two rules that matter more than the caching itself:
  · a null RESULT still counts as computed — do not recompute it
  · the cache is per wrapper, so two Memoize calls share nothing

Then MemoizeTwo, for a function of two arguments, because the
interesting part of a cache is always the KEY.

    MemoizeTwo(Add)(1, 2)   → cached under the pair (1, 2)

hint: Dictionary.TryGetValue tells you "present" and hands you the
value in one lookup. For two arguments, a tuple is already a
perfectly good dictionary key — value equality comes for free.
csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/06-m.explanation:
The cache is a local variable captured by the returned lambda, which
is what makes each wrapper's cache private. Declaring the dictionary
outside Memoize — a static field, say — would make all wrappers share
one, and that is the cache-key collision bug: two callers, one bucket,
and answers that belong to somebody else.
TryGetValue is the right lookup because it answers "is it there?" and
"what is it?" in ONE hash probe, and because it distinguishes a
stored null from a missing entry. `if (cache[key] != null)` gets both
wrong: it throws on a miss and recomputes stored nulls forever.
MemoizeTwo shows why tuples are such good keys: ValueTuple has
structural equality and a combined hash code already, so (1, 2) and
(2, 1) are different keys with no work from you. Concatenating the
arguments into a string — "1:2" — is the classic wrong turn, and it
collides the moment an argument contains the separator.
What this deliberately does NOT do: bound the cache, expire entries,
or handle concurrency. An unbounded memoize on user input is a memory
leak with extra steps. Real caches need a size limit (see the LRU in
module 09) and, for shared use, ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd —
which, note, may still run the factory more than once under a race.

csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/07-e.instructions:
**Concepts:** events · multicast delegates · unsubscribing  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

An event is a multicast delegate with the += and -= doors left open
and everything else locked: only the declaring class may raise it.

Finish the Publisher class at the BOTTOM of this file:

    Publish(message)    calls every subscriber, in order; does
                        nothing (and does NOT throw) with none
    SubscriberCount     how many handlers are attached right now
    Reset()             detach every handler

Publishing to nobody is the normal state of an event, not an error.

hint: an event with no subscribers is null. `Published?.Invoke(...)`
is the safe raise. `Delegate.GetInvocationList()` gives you the
attached handlers as an array — on a null delegate you cannot call
it at all, which is a case worth handling.
csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/07-e.explanation:
A delegate field holding no handlers is NULL, not an empty list, so
`Published(this, m)` throws a NullReferenceException the moment
nobody is listening — which in production is the first minute after
a subscriber is refactored away. `Published?.Invoke(this, m)` is the
idiom, and it also takes a snapshot of the delegate, which is why it
survives another thread unsubscribing mid-raise.
Handlers fire in subscription order and the SAME handler attached
twice fires twice: += appends, it does not deduplicate. That is the
double-fire bug — an event subscribed in a method that runs on every
navigation, never unsubscribed, firing twice, then three times.
-= removes ONE attachment, matching on delegate equality. Two lambdas
with identical bodies are different objects, so `x += (_, _) => f();`
followed by `x -= (_, _) => f();` removes nothing at all. Keep a
reference to the handler you attached — that is why the tests declare
`EventHandler<string> handler` as a variable.
Setting the event to null inside the class detaches everyone at once.
From OUTSIDE the class you cannot do that, cannot invoke it, and
cannot even read it — that is the entire difference between an event
and a public delegate field, and it is why events are safe to expose.
The leak worth remembering: the publisher holds a reference to every
subscriber. A long-lived publisher keeps short-lived subscribers
alive forever. Unsubscribe in Dispose, always.

csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/08-c.instructions:
**Concepts:** currying · partial application · configuration as closure  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

Currying turns a two-argument function into a one-argument function
that returns another one. Partial application fixes an argument now
and leaves the rest for later. Both are the same idea as dependency
injection, minus the container.

    Curry(Add)(1)(2)         → 3
    Uncurry(Curry(Add))(1,2) → 3
    PartialLeft(Add, 10)(5)  → 15

Then the practical version of the same trick: Configure takes a
logger prefix and returns a ready-to-use logging function.

    Configure("api")("boom") → "[api] boom"

hint: every one of these is a lambda returning a lambda. Write the
types out longhand once — Func<T1, Func<T2, TResult>> — and the
bodies become obvious.
csbootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates/08-c.explanation:
Read the type and the body writes itself. Curry must return
Func<T1, Func<T2, TResult>>, so it is `a => b => f(a, b)`: take the
first argument, hand back something that waits for the second.
Uncurry is the inverse, `(a, b) => f(a)(b)`, and the round-trip test
is what proves they really are inverses rather than two functions
that happen to work on ints.
PartialLeft is currying with the first argument already supplied —
the same closure, created eagerly. That is the whole idea behind
configuration: Configure("api") is partial application over a
logging function, and the returned delegate carries its prefix with
it. A constructor that stores a dependency in a field is doing
exactly this, with more ceremony.
Where it pays off in C#: building a validator once and reusing it,
adapting a two-argument API to something that expects
Func<T, TResult>, and pushing configuration to the edge so the inner
function has no idea where its settings came from. Where it does not:
C# has no partial-application syntax, so a chain of three or more
arrows becomes unreadable fast. Past two arguments, take a record.
Watch what is captured. `Configure(prefix)` captures the parameter,
so each call keeps its own — the same per-call capture that made two
Adders independent in exercise 02.
